title: Taking Charge Without Taking Charge
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The distinction drawn here is between taking charge and taking over, and the whole piece hangs on keeping the two apart. Great leaders, on this account, set strategy, choose the metrics that matter, make themselves reachable, and then deliberately step back so that skilled people can do what they already know how to do. The author diagnoses the failure mode as a motivational imbalance rather than a skills gap: some leaders simply need to control outcomes more than they need to see achievement happen. A second distinction sharpens the point — offering support and advice is categorically different from directing action and policing work quality, and leaders who define themselves as the person who holds others accountable end up pushing rather than pulling. The alternative is not passivity; accountability is redefined as regular check-ins, conversations about how people are doing, and visible availability as a resource. The memorable reframe is that team members should feel unable to escape a leader's care rather than their surveillance, and the closing line turns the title inside out: the best leaders take charge of themselves, not of others.
points: The author separates two things usually conflated — setting strategy and metrics, which is the leader's job, from directing action and inspecting quality, which is not.
The controlling leader is explained motivationally: the need to direct specific outcomes outranks the need to facilitate achievement, which is why the behaviour survives good intentions.
Defining oneself as the person who holds others accountable is identified as the specific self-concept that produces pushing instead of pulling, and the resistance that follows.
Accountability is recast as a cadence of check-ins and conversations about the metrics rather than an enforcement posture.
The contrast that closes the argument: leaders who would do anything for others to succeed behave differently from leaders desperate to drive team success, even when both want the same result.
quotes: Winning the support of a team, especially those most skilled and qualified, requires leaders to take charge without taking over.
What this means is that great leaders set strategy, dial up the right metrics, open their door to any inquiry, and then get out of the way.
That’s because their need to direct and control specific outcomes is higher than their need to facilitate achievement.
Accountability for skillful leaders is about consistently checking in, talking about how others are doing, discussing the key metrics, and serving as a resource.
Team members should come to feel they can’t escape the care of a leader rather than their ever-watchful eye.
By remembering that work quality is always a team sport, leaders can come to provide what team members most need from them to be successful.
